subtopics.title: Objects, Types, Mutability, Assignment, and Names
subtopics.summary: Objects have identity, type, and value. Names bind to objects; rebinding changes the name, while mutation only matters for mutable objects.

exam_question_ids: exam-Trial final exam Introduction to Python-3-w1-objects-and-names

related_topics: Objects, Types, Mutability, Assignment, and Names

trap_patterns.trap: l2=l1 vs l2=l1[:] — l2=l1 shares the SAME object, slicing creates independent copy
def f(lst=[]): — the [] is created ONCE at def time and persists across calls. Fix: use None and create inside function
When mutable object passed as argument, parameter and argument point to SAME object — mutations inside function affect original
If a name appears on the left side of assignment ANYWHERE in a function, Python treats it as local THROUGHOUT the function body — even before the assignment line

trap_patterns.pattern: Tuple inside mutable container can be mutated via the mutable part
trap_patterns.trap: t=(1,[2,3],4); t[1].append(5) works — tuple immutable means you can't reassign t[1], but the list t[1] refers to IS mutable
print[1] → TypeError 'not subscriptable'; l1(1) → TypeError 'not callable'
list(map(lambda x: x*2, l)) — must wrap in list(). Without it: <map object at 0x...>
True==1, False==0 in numeric contexts. type(True)==int is False but isinstance(True,int) is True

lecture_snippets.subtopic_title: Objects, Types, Mutability, Assignment, and Names
lecture_snippets.title: Objects: core properties
lecture_snippets.explanation: Every object has exactly one unique id (cannot change), exactly one type (cannot change), and exactly one value. The type defines what value can be stored and whether the value is mutable or immutable. An object can have zero, one, or more names bound to it. A name can only refer to one object at any time.

lecture_snippets.subtopic_title: Objects, Types, Mutability, Assignment, and Names
lecture_snippets.title: Mutable vs immutable types
lecture_snippets.explanation: Immutable: int, float, str, bool, tuple. Mutable: list, dict, set. The value of a mutable object CAN be changed in-place. The value of an immutable object CANNOT be changed — a new object must be created.

code_examples.description: List is mutable — can change element in place
Tuple is immutable — assigning to index raises TypeError
code_examples.code:
t1 = (1, 2, 3)
t1[2] = 4
# TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment

code_examples.description: String reassignment creates a NEW object, not mutation
code_examples.code:
box_1 = 'content'
old_id = id(box_1)
box_1 = 'new content'
new_id = id(box_1)
print(old_id == new_id)  # False — different object

lecture_snippets.subtopic_title: Objects, Types, Mutability, Assignment, and Names
lecture_snippets.title: Assignment statements — reading right to left
lecture_snippets.explanation: Python creates a new object with the value on the right, infers type from the value, then binds the name on the left to that object.

code_examples.code:
name_1 = 300
print(name_1)        # 300
print(type(name_1))  # <class 'int'>
print(id(name_1))    # some unique integer

code_examples.description: Two names bound to the same object (same id)
code_examples.code:
name_3 = name_4 = name_5 = name_6 = 300
print(name_3 is name_4 is name_5 is name_6)  # True

code_examples.description: Two separate objects with equal value (different id)
code_examples.code:
name_1 = 300
name_2 = 300
print(name_1 == name_2)           # True (same value)
print(id(name_1) != id(name_2))   # True (different objects)

lecture_snippets.subtopic_title: Objects, Types, Mutability, Assignment, and Names
lecture_snippets.title: Names / variable naming rules
lecture_snippets.explanation: Names can consist of letters (upper/lower), digits, and underscores. Names CANNOT start with a digit. Names ARE case-sensitive (name_1 != Name_1). Avoid Python reserved words (e.g., don't name a variable 'sorted', 'list', 'print').

lecture_snippets.subtopic_title: Objects, Types, Mutability, Assignment, and Names
lecture_snippets.title: Slicing
lecture_snippets.explanation: Syntax: seq[start:end:step]. Start is inclusive, end is NOT inclusive. Defaults: start=0, end=len, step=1. Negative step goes from right to left. Slicing always creates a NEW object of the same type.

code_examples.description: Slicing creates new object — key exam trap
code_examples.code:
l1 = [1, 2, 3, 4]
l2 = l1
l3 = l1[:]
l1[-1] = 5
print(l1 == l2, l2 == l3)  # True False (l3 is independent copy)

code_examples.description: Changing a list slice vs index
code_examples.code:
l1 = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
l1[1:2] = [1, 1]      # replaces element at index 1 with two elements
print(l1)             # [1, 1, 1, 3, 4, 5, 6]

l1 = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
l1[1] = [1, 1]        # replaces element at index 1 with a list
print(l1)             # [1, [1, 1], 3, 4, 5, 6]

t1 = (1, 2, 3)
print(t1[1:])          # (2, 3)
s1 = 'uva Amsterdam'
print(s1[5:-3:2])      # 'mtr'

s1 = 'uva Amsterdam'
# s1[6] = 's'  # ERROR
s1 = s1[:6] + 's' + s1[7:]
print(s1)  # works

t1 = (1, 4, 3)
# t1[1] = 2  # ERROR
t1 = t1[:1] + (2,) + t1[2:]
print(t1)  # works

lecture_snippets.title: objects
lecture_snippets.explanation:
### Everything in Python is an object. Objects in Python have one id, one value, one type, and zero or more names
An assignment statement is one of the ways to create an object. An object created with an assignment statement will have a name, an id, a value and a type.

exam_questions.question:
Suppose you have the following function:
def multiply(*args, factor=2):
total = 1
for num in args:
total *= num
return total * factor
Which of the following functions will return the same values as the function above, if we call the function thrice as follows:
multiply(1, 2, factor=3)
multiply(3, 4)
multiply()
A def multiply(*args, factor=2):
total = args[0]
for num in args:
total *= num
return total * factor
B def multiply(*args, factor=2):
if not args:
return 0
total = args[0]
for num in args[1:]:
total *= num
return total * factor
C Both functions will return the same values.
D Neither functions will return the same values.

exam_questions.question:
Imagine that you have a list called students, which is populated by a number of dictionaries.

Each dictionary in the students list has two keys: "Name" and "Grade". The corresponding values are student names (as strings) and course grades (as floats).

For each student, you'd like to print the following text to the screen:
[NAME] has received a grade of [GRADE].
where [NAME] is substituted by the name of the student and [GRADE] is substituted by the actual course grade. The course grade should be displayed to one decimal place after the decimal point.

For example, if
students = [{"Name": "Adam", "Grade": 7.5}, {"Name": "Bernard", "Grade": 8.0}]
then you'd like to see the following two lines printed to the screen:
Adam has received a grade of 7.5.
Bernard has received a grade of 8.0.

Which of the following code segments will achieve what you want?

options.a:
for student in students:
    print(f"{student['Name']} has received a grade of {student['Grade']:.1f}.")
options.b:
for student, grade in students.items():
    print(f"{student} has received a grade of {grade:.1f}.")
options.c:
for student in students:
    print(f"{student["Name"]} has received a grade of {student["Grade"]:.1f}.")
options.d:
for student, grade in students:
    print(f'{student} has received a grade of {grade:.1f}.')

exam_questions.explanation: Option A correctly iterates over the list of dictionaries and uses f-strings with proper quote escaping (single quotes inside double quotes) and the `:.1f` format specifier to display the float to one decimal place.

lecture_snippets.title: Arithmetic operators
lecture_snippets.explanation: a+b, a-b, a*b: standard. a/b: always returns float. a//b: floor division (highest integer <= result). a%b: remainder. a**b: exponentiation. NOTE: ^ is NOT exponentiation in Python (it is XOR). (a//b)*b + a%b == a always.

lecture_snippets.subtopic_title: Arithmetic, Comparison, and Boolean Operators
lecture_snippets.title: Comparison operators
lecture_snippets.explanation: ==, !=, >, <, >=, <=. Always return True or False. Comparing floats can be tricky: 1.1+2.2 != 3.3 in Python due to floating-point precision. String/tuple/list comparison is element-by-element left to right; first differing element decides; if equal length and no differences, they are equal; shorter sequence is 'less than' longer if all elements match up to shorter length.

code_examples.code: print(1.1 + 2.2 == 3.3)  # False

print([1, 2, 3] < [1, 2, 3, 0])  # True (shorter is less)
print([2] < [1, 2, 3, 0])        # False (2 > 1 at index 0)

lecture_snippets.subtopic_title: Arithmetic, Comparison, and Boolean Operators
lecture_snippets.title: Boolean operators
lecture_snippets.explanation: x and y: True only if both True. x or y: False only if both False. not x: inverts. NOTE: && and || are Python operators but do something different (bitwise). Precedence: 'not' first, then 'and', then 'or'. Use parentheses to avoid confusion.

code_examples.code:
a=1; b=3
print(a==1 or a==2 and b==1 or b==2)  # True (WRONG: and binds tighter)
print((a==1 or a==2) and (b==1 or b==2))  # False (CORRECT)

bracket_3 = 95000 - 45000

+ (bracket_1 * rate_1)

total_tax = ((gross_income - 45000) * rate_3) + (bracket_2 * rate_2) + (bracket_1 * rate_1)
elif 45000 >= gross_income > 11000:
total_tax = ((gross_income - 11000) * rate_2) + (bracket_1 * rate_1)
else:
total_tax = gross_income * rate_1
net_income = gross_income - total_tax
results['total_tax'] = round(total_tax, 2)
results['net_income'] = round(net_income, 2)
return results

exam_questions.question:
Suppose you have a list called x. Which of the following code segments will print the following list?
[5, 4, 3, 2, 1]

options.a:
y = list(set(x))
print(sorted(y, reverse = True))
options.b: print(x[::-2])
options.c: Both lines of code will print that output.
options.d: Neither line of code will print that output.

exam_questions.explanation: Option A extracts unique elements with `set(x)`, resulting in `{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}`, then sorts them in reverse order, giving `[5, 4, 3, 2, 1]`. Option B uses list slicing `x[::-2]` which steps backwards through `x` by 2, retrieving indices -1, -3, -5, -7, and -9, which correspond to 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. Thus, both A and B are correct.

lecture_snippets.subtopic_title: Creation, Lookup, Updates, and Key Constraints
lecture_snippets.title: Dictionaries
lecture_snippets.explanation: Sets of key:value pairs. Keys must be unique and immutable (hashable). Dictionaries are unordered for equality ({1:1,2:2}=={2:2,1:1} is True). Cannot be sorted. You can check membership with 'in' — this checks KEYS only. Keys() gives key sequence, values() gives value sequence, items() gives tuples.

code_examples.code:
capitals = {}
capitals = dict()
capitals = {'Andorra': 'Andorra la Vella', 'Belgium': 'Brussels'}
print(capitals['Belgium'])         # Brussels
del(capitals['Belgium'])           # delete key
capitals['Netherlands'] = 'Amsterdam'  # insert/update
capitals.update({'France': 'Paris'})   # insert/update multiple

code_examples.description: Dict membership checks KEYS, not values

lecture_snippets.subtopic_title: Creation, Lookup, Updates, and Key Constraints
lecture_snippets.title: Looping over dictionaries
lecture_snippets.explanation: .keys() → key sequence. .values() → value sequence. .items() → sequence of (key, value) tuples. 'for key in dict' is the same as 'for key in dict.keys()'.

lecture_snippets.title: Lists vs Dictionaries vs Sets — ordered/unordered
lecture_snippets.explanation: Lists, tuples, strings are SEQUENCES (ordered). Dicts and sets are NOT sequences (unordered for equality). All are called collections.

code_examples.code:
print([1,2] == [2,1])        # False (ordered)
print((1,2) == (2,1))        # False (ordered)
print('12' == '21')          # False (ordered)
print({1,2} == {2,1})        # True  (unordered)
print({1:1,2:2}=={2:2,1:1})  # True  (unordered)

lecture_snippets.subtopic_title: Sequences, Uniqueness, and Common Operations
lecture_snippets.title: Sets
lecture_snippets.explanation: Unordered collection of unique values. Empty set MUST be set() — {} creates empty dict. Elements must be immutable. No indexing. Methods: .add(), .remove(), .update().

code_examples.code:
countries = set()           # empty set (NOT {})
countries = {'Andorra', 'Belgium'}
print({1,2,2} == {2,1})     # True (duplicates ignored)
print(len({1,2,2}))         # 2
countries.remove('Andorra')
countries.add('Greece')
countries.update({'Spain', 'Italy'})

exam_questions.question:
Suppose you have the following function:

def func1(l1):
    return len(list(l1))==len(set(l1))

Which of the functions below returns the same values as the function above, if we call it in any of the following ways?

func1(l1 = [1,2,3])
func1(l1 = [1,2,2])
func1(l1 = (1,2,2))

options.c: Neither function returns the same values.
options.d: Both functions return the same values.

exam_questions.explanation: Option a: for (1,2,2), tuple has no .count() — wait, actually tuples DO have .count(). For [1,2,2]: element 2 has count>1 so counter=2, returns False. Original returns False. But for a tuple (1,2,2): tuple has .count(), works. But option b: l1[l1.index(element)+1:] — tuples support slicing and indexing too. Let's re-examine: for a tuple (1,2,2), both a and b should work the same. Actually option a counts ALL duplicated elements (counts 2 twice for [1,2,2]), making counter=2, so counter==0 is False. Original is False too. Both match. For option b applied to tuple: l1[l1.index(element)+1:] works for tuples too. Actually both a and b return same values as original. Correct: d.

lecture_snippets.explanation: Precedence (high to low): comparisons → not → and → or. Use parentheses to be explicit. 'in' checks membership in sequence/set/dict-keys.

print(1 in (1,2,3))    # True
print('1' in '123')    # True (substring)

exam_questions.question:
You're trying to write a function called is_anagram, which takes two strings as inputs and checks whether they are anagrams of each other. That is: whether one of them can be written by rearranging the letters of the other. Upper case and lower case versions of a letter count as the same letter, and whitespace characters don't count at all.

For example, the following function calls should all return the boolean value True:
is_anagram("Old West Action", "Clint Eastwood")
is_anagram("eleven plus two", "twelve plus one")
is_anagram("I am a weakish speller", "William Shakespeare")

while the following function call should return the boolean value False:
is_anagram("one plus two", "three")

Which of the following code segments achieves what you want?

options.a:
def is_anagram(word_1, word_2):
    return sorted(list(word_1.replace(" ", "").lower())) == sorted(list(word_2.replace(" ", "").lower()))
options.b:
def is_anagram(word_1, word_2):
    return word_1.replace(" ", "").lower().sort() == word_2.replace(" ", "").lower().sort()
options.c:
def is_anagram(word_1, word_2):
    return list(word_1.replace(" ", "").lower()).sort() == list(word_2.replace(" ", "").lower()).sort()
options.d:
def is_anagram(word_1, word_2):
    return sorted(list(word_1)).replace(" ", "").lower() == sorted(list(word_2)).replace(" ", "").lower()

exam_questions.explanation: Option A correctly removes spaces, converts to lowercase, lists characters, sorts them, and compares the results. Option B and C use .sort() which returns None, and D uses .replace() on a list.

items.summary: What is the difference between `break` and `continue` inside a loop?
items.detail: `break` exits the loop immediately; `continue` skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one.

items.summary: When do you reach for `enumerate` versus `zip`?

key_points_to_remember.text: Use `for` when you already have an iterable; use `while` when repetition should continue only while a condition stays `True`.
`break` exits the loop immediately; `continue` skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one.
`enumerate(seq, start)` gives `(index, value)` pairs; `zip(a, b)` gives tuples of items from multiple iterables in parallel.
A `while` condition is checked before every iteration, so a list loop like `while items:` keeps going only while the list is non-empty.

lecture_snippets.subtopic_title: Explicit Conversion and Truthy/Falsy Rules
lecture_snippets.title: Truthy and Falsy
lecture_snippets.explanation: In conditions, Python auto-converts to bool. Falsy: [], (), {}, set(), '', 0, 0.0, range(0), None. Truthy: everything else (non-empty collections, non-zero numbers).

code_examples.code:
# All evaluate to False in a condition:
[]    # empty list
()    # empty tuple

set() # empty set
''    # empty string

lecture_snippets.subtopic_title: Explicit Conversion and Truthy/Falsy Rules
lecture_snippets.title: Type conversion (explicit)
lecture_snippets.explanation: Python requires explicit conversion in most cases (unlike JavaScript). Conversion functions: str(), int(), float(), bool(), tuple(), list(), set(), dict().

code_examples.code:
print(str(1) == '1')           # True
print(int('1') == 1)           # True
print(int('1a'))               # ERROR
print(float('1') == 1.0)       # True
print(float('1.0') == 1.0)     # True
print(tuple([1,2,3]) == (1,2,3)) # True
print(tuple({1:3, 2:4}) == (1,2)) # True (dict->tuple gives keys)
print(list(range(1,5,2)) == [1,3]) # True
print(dict([1, 2]))            # ERROR
print(dict([(1,3),(2,4)]) == {1:3, 2:4})  # True

code_examples.description: Implicit conversion (Python allows with bool/numeric mix)
code_examples.code:
print(1 + True)    # 2
print(1.0 + False) # 1.0
print('1' * 2)     # '11'
print('1' * True)  # '1'
print('1' * False) # ''

lecture_snippets.subtopic_title: def, Calls, and Methods vs Functions
lecture_snippets.title: Methods vs functions
lecture_snippets.explanation: Methods are functions attached to objects. Calling obj.method() is equivalent to Class.method(obj). For mutable objects: some methods CHANGE the object (e.g. list.sort()), some RETURN a value (e.g. list.index()). For immutable objects: methods always return a new value (can't change the object itself). COMMON ERROR: s1.upper() on strings — you must do s1 = s1.upper() to save the result.

code_examples.description: Method on immutable — must capture return value
code_examples.code:
s1 = 'UVA Amsterdam'
s1 = s1.upper()  # CORRECT — captures new string
s1.upper()       # WRONG — result is lost, s1 unchanged

code_examples.description: Method on mutable — changes in place vs returns value
code_examples.code:
l1 = [3, 1, 2]
l1.sort()           # changes l1 in place, returns None
print(l1)           # [1, 2, 3]
print(l1.index(2))  # 1 (returns index, doesn't change l1)

exam_questions.question:
You would like to write a function called get_tld that extracts the top-level domain from the URL of a website. The function takes the URL as the input string in the following format:
"https://www.[SECOND-LEVEL DOMAIN].[TOP-LEVEL DOMAIN]/[FOLDER 1]/[...]/[FOLDER N]/[PAGE NAME].html"
and returns the top-level domain as a string.

For example, the function call:
get_tld("https://www.uva.nl/en/education/bachelor-s/bachelors.html")
should return the string:
"nl"

Which of the following code segments would not achieve what you want?

options.b:
def get_tld(url):
    url_1 = url.split("//")[1]
    url_2 = url_1.split("/")[0]
    return url_2.split(".")[-1]
options.c:
def get_tld(url):
    return url.split("//")[1].split("/")[0].split(".")[-1]
options.d:
def get_tld(url):
    url_1 = url[url.find("//") + 2:]
    url_2 = url_1.split("/")[0]
    return url_2.split(".")[-1]

exam_questions.explanation: Option A splits the entire URL by '.', so the last element will be 'html' (from 'bachelors.html'). Then splitting 'html' by '/' and taking the first element still results in 'html', not the top-level domain 'nl'. Therefore, it does NOT achieve what is intended.

exam_questions.question:
You're trying to write a function called is_anagram, which takes two strings as inputs and checks whether they are anagrams of each other. That is: whether one of them can be written by rearranging the letters of the other. Upper case and lower case versions of a letter count as the same letter, and whitespace characters don't count at all.

For example, the following function calls should all return the boolean value True:
is_anagram("Old West Action", "Clint Eastwood")
is_anagram("eleven plus two", "twelve plus one")
is_anagram("I am a weakish speller", "William Shakespeare")

while the following function call should return the boolean value False:
is_anagram("one plus two", "three")

Which of the following code segments achieves what you want?

options.a:
def is_anagram(word_1, word_2):
    return sorted(list(word_1.replace(" ", "").lower())) == sorted(list(word_2.replace(" ", "").lower()))
options.b:
def is_anagram(word_1, word_2):
    return word_1.replace(" ", "").lower().sort() == word_2.replace(" ", "").lower().sort()
options.c:
def is_anagram(word_1, word_2):
    return list(word_1.replace(" ", "").lower()).sort() == list(word_2.replace(" ", "").lower()).sort()
options.d:
def is_anagram(word_1, word_2):
    return sorted(list(word_1)).replace(" ", "").lower() == sorted(list(word_2)).replace(" ", "").lower()

exam_questions.explanation: Option A correctly removes spaces, converts strings to lower case, transforms them to lists, and sorts the lists using sorted() before comparing them. Option B is incorrect because strings do not have a .sort() method. Option C is incorrect because list.sort() operates in-place and returns None, so it would compare None == None. Option D is incorrect because sorted() returns a list, and lists do not have a .replace() or .lower() method.

exam_questions.question:
You need to write a function called format_phone_number that formats phone numbers. The output of the function should be a string that represents a 10-digit number. The input argument is also a string with 10 digits, but the digits may be separated by dashes (the "-" character) at various places.

For example, the following function calls:
format_phone_number("020-525-1400")
format_phone_number("020-5251400")
format_phone_number("020-525-14-00")
should all return the string:
"0205251400"

Which of the following code segments does not achieve what you want?

options.b:
def format_phone_number(number):
    return number.replace("-", "")
options.d:
def format_phone_number(number):
    return "".join(number.split("-"))

exam_questions.explanation: Strings in Python are immutable. The `replace()` method returns a new string, it does not modify the original string in place. Because Option A does not reassign the result of `number.replace("-", "")` or return it directly, it returns the original, unmodified string.

subtopics.title: Global vs Local Names and Scope Errors
subtopics.summary: Assignment inside a function creates a local name unless `global` or `nonlocal` says otherwise. Reading a local before assignment raises `UnboundLocalError`.

related_topics: Global vs Local Names and Scope Errors

trap_patterns.trap: If a name appears on the left side of assignment ANYWHERE in a function, Python treats it as local THROUGHOUT the function body — even before the assignment line

lecture_snippets.subtopic_title: Global vs Local Names and Scope Errors
lecture_snippets.title: Global and local scope
lecture_snippets.explanation: Local names: defined inside a function (parameter names + any assignment inside). Only known inside the function. Global names: defined outside any function, known everywhere EXCEPT when a same-named local exists (local dominates). Python makes names local at call time, BEFORE executing the body — so if you assign to a name ANYWHERE in a function, that name is local throughout the function (even before the assignment line). Use 'global' keyword to override (but avoid it).

code_examples.code:
def adder(n1, n2):
    return n1 + n2
adder(1, 2)
print(n1)  # NameError: name 'n1' is not defined

code_examples.description: UnboundLocalError trap — local shadows global even before assignment
code_examples.code:
def main(a):
    b = b      # ERROR: Python sees b assigned in function -> local
    return a   # but local b has no value yet
b = 1
print(main(1))  # UnboundLocalError

def changer():
    global n1
    n1 = n1 + 1
n1 = 1
changer()
print(n1)  # 2

def changer(n1):
    n1 = n1 + 1
    return n1
a = 1
a = changer(a)
print(a)  # 2

code_examples.description: Mutable parameter is the SAME object
code_examples.code:
def adder(l2):
    result = 0
    while l2:
        result += l2.pop()
    return result
l1 = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
total = adder(l1)
print(f'The sum of {l1} = {total}')  # The sum of [] = 15 !!!
# l1 is empty because l2 and l1 refer to the SAME list object

exam_questions.question:
val = 2
def func():
    val = 3
    print(val)
func()
print(val)

Which of the following code snippets produces the same output as the above code snippet?

options.a:
val1 = 2
def func1():
    val1 = val1 + 1
    print(val1)
func1()
print(val1)
options.b:
val2 = 2
def func2():
    global val2
    val2 = val2 + 1
    print(val2)
func2()
print(val2)
options.c:
val3 = 2
def func3():
    val3 = 3
    def innerfunc():
        val3 = 2
        print(val3)
    print(val3)
func3()
print(val3)
options.d:
val4 = 2
def func4():
    val4 = 3
    def innerfunc():
        val4 = 2
        print(val4)
    print(val4)
func4()
innerfunc()

'var_2 = var_1 - var'
This line produces the error because func_2() was not called and assigning the value to var_1, thus, var_1 was referenced before being defined.
options.b:
'var_1 = var * 2'
This line produces the error because Python is confused about which value var should have.
options.c:
'def func_2(var):'

ai_summary.content: Assignment inside a function creates a local name unless `global` or `nonlocal` says otherwise. Reading a local before assignment raises `UnboundLocalError`.

bullets: Which other program will give the same output as the following code snippet?
Which other program will produce the same output as the following code snippet?

val = 2
def func():
    val = 3
    print(val)
func()
print(val)

Which of the following code snippets produces the same output as the above code snippet?
Calling the function func_1() will produce an error. Which line of the following code segment produces the error?
If a name appears on the left side of assignment ANYWHERE in a function, Python treats it as local THROUGHOUT the function body — even before the assignment line

items.summary: Why does `print(n1)` fail outside `def adder(n1, n2): ...`?
items.detail: Parameter names are local to the function body, so they do not exist in the global scope after the call finishes.
items.code:
def adder(n1, n2):
    return n1 + n2

adder(1, 2)
print(n1)

items.summary: Why can assigning to a name inside a function cause `UnboundLocalError`?
items.detail: If a function assigns to a name anywhere in its body, Python treats that name as local throughout the function unless you declare it `global` or `nonlocal`.
items.code:
b = 1

def main(a):
    b = b
    return a

items.summary: When do you need `global`?
items.detail: Use `global name` only when the function should rebind a global variable; simple reads of a global name do not need it.
items.code:
n1 = 1

def changer():
    global n1
    n1 = n1 + 1

key_points_to_remember.text: Names assigned inside a function are local by default, including parameter names.
If a function assigns to a name anywhere, Python treats that name as local throughout that function unless `global` or `nonlocal` says otherwise.
Use `global x` only when the function should rebind the global name `x`; mutating an object passed in as an argument does not require `global`.

lecture_snippets.title: *args — undefined number of positional arguments
lecture_snippets.explanation: Prefixing a parameter with * makes Python collect all extra positional arguments into a tuple named args. Can mix with defined parameters: def f(n1, n2, *args) — Python fills n1,n2 first then collects remainder into args.

lecture_snippets.title: Keyword arguments and **kwargs

lecture_snippets.subtopic_title: Positional, Keyword, Default, *args, **kwargs, and Mutable Argument Traps
lecture_snippets.title: Default arguments
lecture_snippets.explanation: Default values are part of the function HEADER (not the call). When argument is omitted, the default is used. Keyword args in a call use =. CRITICAL: mutable defaults are evaluated ONCE at def time — never use mutable defaults; use None instead.

code_examples.code:
def multiplier(first, second=2):
    return first * second
print(multiplier(3))       # 6 (uses default second=2)
print(multiplier(3, 3))    # 9
print(multiplier(2, second=3))  # 6

def main(addition, l1=[]):
    l1.append(addition)
    return l1
print(main(2))  # [2]
print(main(3))  # [2, 3] ← BUG: l1 persists!

def main(addition, l1=None):
    if l1 is None:
        l1 = []
    l1 += [addition]
    return l1
print(main(2))  # [2]
print(main(3))  # [3]  ← correct

return info
B      def print_info(**kwargs, name, age):

info['age'] = age
return info

Which of the following functions will achieve what you need?

y = {}

x['smallest'] = min(y)
x['largest'] = max(y)
x['total'] = sum(y)
return x
B      def summarize(x):
y = {}
total = 0
for integer in x:
y['amount'] = len(x)
if integer == min(x):
y['smallest'] = min(x)
elif integer == max(x):
y['largest'] = max(x)
else:
y['total'] += integer
return y
C      def summarize(x):
y = {}
for integer in x:
if integer == min(x):
y['smallest'] == min(x)
elif integer == max(x):
y['largest'] == max(x)
else:
y['amount'] == x.count()
y['total'] == sum(x)
return y

lecture_snippets.title: Lambda functions
lecture_snippets.explanation: Anonymous one-line functions. Syntax: lambda params: expression. Equivalent to a regular def but more concise. Most useful with map, filter, reduce, sorted, max.

code_examples.code:

from functools import reduce
l1 = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
print(reduce(lambda x, y: x*y, l1))  # 720 (product)
# reduce with initial value:
l1 = ['aaa', 'baab', 'c']
print(reduce(lambda x, y: x + y.count('a'), l1, 0))  # 5

print(sorted(l1, key=len))                    # ['c', 'aaa', 'baab']

d = {'a': 2, 'b': 1}

print(max(d.items(), key=lambda x: x[1]))     # ('a', 2)  ← by value

exam_questions.question:
Given the class definition above, trying to execute the following two code lines will result in a Python error.
my_flight = Flight("KLM", "Amsterdam", "Paris")                     # Code line 1
my_flight.set_date(my_flight, "29-02-2022")                         # Code line 2

Why?

options.a: The first argument (my_flight) should not have been passed to the set_date method in Code line 2.
options.b: The capacity of the flight is not specified as an argument in Code line 1.
options.c: The argument self is missing in Code line 1.
options.d: The date string passed as an argument in Code line 2 represents an invalid date.

exam_questions.explanation: In Python, when calling a method on an object, the object itself is automatically passed as the first argument (self). Passing my_flight explicitly results in too many arguments being passed to set_date.

exam_questions.subtopic_title: Class Definition, __init__, self, and Attribute Basics
exam_questions.question:
Suppose that you also want to write a method called compare that compares the book to another book and gives a recommendation for which one to read. A book is better than another book if its average review score is higher than the second book's and it has at least as many reviews as the second book.

The compare method should return the title of the better book. If neither book is better than the other, then it should return None.

For simplicity, you can assume that both books have at least one review already.

Which method definition achieves what you want?

options.c: Both methods above compare the book objects as intended.
options.d: Neither of the two methods above compare the book objects as intended.

exam_questions.explanation: Option A fails because its 'elif not avg_better:' condition triggers simply when the other book has an equal or better score, but it returns the other book's title without checking if the other book has at least as many reviews as the first book. Option B checks both pairs (self, other) and (other, self) against the requirements, returning the better one, or implicitly returning None if neither is better.

class Rectangle:
    total_size = 0
    def __init__(self, length, width=1):
        self.length = length
        self.width = width
        Rectangle.total_size += self.length * self.width
        print(f'{self.length} by {self.width} created, {Rectangle.total_size = }')
    def size(self, data_type=int):
        return f"The size = {data_type(self.length * self.width)}."
    def __del__(self):
        Rectangle.total_size -= self.length * self.width
        print(f'{self.length} by {self.width} deleted, {Rectangle.total_size = }')

exam_questions.subtopic_title: Series, DataFrame, and Creation Patterns
exam_questions.question:
You have a pandas Series called s, which contains floats. You'd like to create a new Series, in which each element is equal to the square of the difference between the corresponding element in s and the mean of the elements in s.

For example, if s is the Series:
0     2.0
1     2.0
2     3.0
3     5.0
dtype: float64

then you want the new Series to be:
0     1.0
1     1.0
2     0.0
3     4.0
dtype: float64

Which of the following code segments does not achieve what you want?

options.a: s.map((s - s.mean())**2)
options.b: (s - s.mean())**2
options.c: s.map(lambda x: (x - s.mean())**2)
options.d: (s - s.mean()).map(lambda x: x**2)

exam_questions.explanation: The map() method on a Series expects a function, dictionary, or another Series. If passed a Series, it uses the values of the caller (s) to look up indices in the passed Series. This will lead to unexpected results (looking up float values like 2.0 as indices) instead of applying the mathematical transformation. The other options correctly perform the element-wise operation.

exam_questions.question:
You have a pandas DataFrame called df that looks like this, when printed:

      A    B    C    D
1  9.1  9.5  9.0  6.0
2  6.4  8.2  7.5  1.7
3  2.5  5.3  8.8  3.0
4  6.7  3.6  7.2  6.9
5  8.4  1.9  8.2  3.3
6  8.1  8.4  9.9  2.2

Suppose that you'd like to create a new DataFrame that only contains those elements of column "B" in df that have an even-numbered index. Which of the following code lines will achieve what you want?

options.a: df.loc[df.index % 2 == 0, ["B"]]

exam_questions.explanation: Option A uses boolean indexing (`df.index % 2 == 0`) to select rows with even index values, and specifically selects column "B" using `.loc`.

exam_questions.subtopic_title: head, tail, describe, loc, iloc, Result Types, and Boolean Indexing
exam_questions.question: Suppose that you'd like to create a new DataFrame that contains only column 'B' for rows with indices 2, 4, and 6. Which of the following code lines will achieve what you want?
exam_questions.explanation: Option A uses a boolean mask on the index to find even numbers and specifies ['B'] as a list to return a DataFrame. Option D would return a Series.

trap_patterns.trap: l2=l1 vs l2=l1[:] — l2=l1 shares the SAME object, slicing creates independent copy
def f(lst=[]): — the [] is created ONCE at def time and persists across calls. Fix: use None and create inside function
When mutable object passed as argument, parameter and argument point to SAME object — mutations inside function affect original
4 in {1:4, 2:3} → False (4 is a value, not a key)

trap_patterns.pattern: Boolean operator precedence: not > and > or
trap_patterns.trap: a==1 or a==2 and b==1 or b==2 is evaluated as a==1 or (a==2 and b==1) or b==2
Function without return statement, or where return is not reached, returns None. print(func()) will print None.
If a name appears on the left side of assignment ANYWHERE in a function, Python treats it as local THROUGHOUT the function body — even before the assignment line

notebook_snippets.title: def generatorfunction(start, stop, step):
notebook_snippets.source:
def generatorfunction(start, stop, step):
    while (num:=start) <= stop:
        yield num
        start += step
    return 'End of numbers'
mygenerator = generatorfunction(1, 5, 2)

items.summary: When do you use `strftime` versus `strptime`?
items.detail: `strftime` formats a datetime into text; `strptime` parses text into a datetime object.
items.code:
dt.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')
datetime.strptime('2024-05-20', '%Y-%m-%d')

items.summary: Which attributes exist directly on a `timedelta` object?
items.detail: A `timedelta` stores `days`, `seconds`, and `microseconds`; hours or weeks must be derived or supplied when constructing it.
items.code:
delta = end - start
print(delta.days, delta.seconds)

items.summary: How can you compute the day number within the year from a datetime?
items.detail: Subtract January 1st of the same year, take `.days`, and add 1 so January 1st becomes day 1.
items.code:
def day_of_year(dt):
    return (dt - datetime(dt.year, 1, 1)).days + 1

key_points_to_remember.text: `datetime.now()` gives the current local datetime; use `.timestamp()` only when you specifically need seconds since the Unix epoch.
`strftime` formats a datetime into text; `strptime` parses text into a datetime object.
Subtracting two datetimes gives a `timedelta`; its most-used direct attributes are `.days`, `.seconds`, and `.microseconds`.
Datetime objects are immutable, so `.replace(...)` returns a new datetime instead of modifying the original one.

ai_examples.title: Check whether two datetime intervals overlap
ai_examples.code:
from datetime import datetime

start_a = datetime(2024, 5, 20, 9, 0)
end_a = datetime(2024, 5, 20, 11, 0)
start_b = datetime(2024, 5, 20, 10, 30)
end_b = datetime(2024, 5, 20, 12, 0)

overlaps = max(start_a, start_b) < min(end_a, end_b)
print(overlaps)
ai_examples.why: A reliable overlap check compares the later start with the earlier end; there is overlap only when the later start is still before the earlier end.
